Regarding the "Explanation of the Objects of Affliction": from this point downward, the six objects explicitly presented in the text and the three objects summarized therein are all [objects] that have been activated and attained.
These nine objects are external to those from which afflictions arise, extending even to the Four Great Vows.
They belong solely to the objective realm (*viṣaya*) and are subsumed under the three aggregates (*skandha*).

Therefore, even when ordinary [beings] are not devoid of afflictions (*kleśa*) up until the moment they resolve their minds for awakening (*cittotpāda*), these must all be regarded as objects; it is not that they are not called objects.
The present text is intended to clarify the contemplation of the aggregates (*skandha*) and the resulting attainments;
therefore, it is necessary to distinguish its differences [from other traditions].
May readers and practitioners not become confused regarding our own fundamental school.
As stated in the previous analysis of the seven categories,
these ten objects are said to be subsumed under the three obstacles; however,
they are not themselves the three obstacles that arise in the present moment.
Regarding the manifestation of the three obstacles,
as stated in the tenth fascicle of the Mahāvaipulya Sūtra:
"When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas seek the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā)..."
It is for the purpose of eliminating the three kinds of obstructions for sentient beings.
As for the obstruction of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*),
it refers to the entanglements of the three poisons, the eight coverings, the eight types of pride, the four perversions, and so forth.
Karmic obstructions refer to the retribution of the five deeds of immediate retribution;
obstructions of retribution refer to those in the three evil realms, as well as those who slander the true Dharma and the icchantikas.
Thus we know that raising up evil can act as an obstruction;
therefore, it is called an "obstruction" (*āvaraṇa*).
Now, by means of their common category, the latter two are subsumed under this.
In the initial section explaining the general purpose of the coming [of this treatise],
first the preceding [section] is concluded and the subsequent one is introduced;
"the upper" [refers to] the conclusion of the preceding [section].
After observing the subsequent section on "descending birth," the preceding section on "condemning desire" correctly clarifies the underlying intent. First,
let us briefly distinguish it from the various preceding passages.
There is the combination of the Dharma and the analogy.
First, it clarifies the distinction from the "reproving of desire and discarding of hindrances" within the preceding section on skillful means.
Next, it clarifies the distinction from the "objects of the aggregates" (*skandha*) mentioned above.
Regarding the desire for the upper realms and within the sense bases (*āyatana*),
although there are signs of delusion, they have not yet reached a state of excessive intensity and thus do not constitute the objective sphere of the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Therefore, among the condemnations of desire, one should understand that the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) are the conditions that give rise to the craving of a practitioner.
The arising of desire is a fault;
because faults give rise to transgressions, they must be censured.
Among the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), these are merely defilements that have fallen away from conditions which obstruct entry into contemplation.
One must abandon them.
Furthermore, if these two sets of five are either censured or discarded,
they merely constitute skillful means and do not yet constitute the actual application of contemplation.
Previously, when observing the aggregates (*skandha*) and sense bases (*āyatana*), one contemplates the resultant aggregates (*vipākaskandha*).
Since the resultant aggregates are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), one seeks a sublime understanding regarding those aggregates;
therefore, the objects of those aggregates are not yet termed afflictions (*kleśa*).
Furthermore, although the previous section on the detailed examination of a single mind observed greed and hatred,
this was not intended as the present object of focus;
rather, it concerned the various currently manifest afflictions, both wholesome and unwholesome.
All are subsumed within the aggregates (skandha) and bases (āyatana).
Therefore, the afflictions that arise because of the aggregates are all termed "objects of the aggregates" (skandhaviṣaya).
Now, the present object must necessarily arise from the contemplation of the aggregates;
only when it gives rise to intense greed and so forth is it designated as the "present object.
From this point onward, one proceeds with the contemplation.
This correctly raises the point that the present object differs from the aggregates (skandhas), hindrances (nīvaraṇas), and so forth;
hence it says, "giving rise to intense greed and hatred.
The phrase "like iron falling" introduces a simile.
Iron is like the latent dispositions (anuśaya), and contemplation (vipaśyanā) is like the fire.
Because the latent dispositions have not yet encountered contemplation, the long-dormant delusions remain hidden;
therefore, it is said that they are merely black.
Because one observes the realm of the aggregates (*skandha*) but the understanding of the aggregates has not yet arisen,
and because the arising of practice differs from what preceded it, it is called "suddenly manifest" (*he ran*).
Furthermore, following the section on the retributive dharma (*vipāka-dharma*), the next part distinguishes between the difficult and the easy.
Furthermore, by restating the *kāmacchanda-nīvaraṇa* (hindrance of sensual desire) along with the *skandhas* and *āyatanas*,
we shall collectively examine the ease or difficulty of [overcoming] the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the present.
Therefore, the essential nature of the hindrance of sensual desire pervasively belongs to the *skandhas* and *āyatanas*.
Therefore, it is given the common name "ordinary" (*sāmānya*) together with the aggregates (*skandha*) and bases (*āyatana*).
Why? This is because the following provides a specific explanation, contrasting its difficulty or ease with the three preceding dharmas.
In the initial clarification of the mutual correspondence, there is first the teaching and then the analogy.
Within the teaching, the three preceding poisons are brought forth to be contrasted with the present ones;
the former are retributive phenomena and manifest afflictions.
Therefore, it is easy to cease;
but now that it has arisen with such intensity, it is difficult to restrain.
Inverted perception is delusion.
The greedy person can be seen.

She transformed herself into a woman and lured him to where her horse was;
then she vanished from sight.
His lust became so intense that he knew no bounds.
Below this, the auxiliary conditions for these afflictions are further analyzed.
The afflictions already aroused exceed their normal state;

Now, by using a wooden paddle, one strikes that swift current, causing the water to contract and ripples to arise.

Next, regarding the initial explanation of the characteristics within the formal commentary:
first, within the explanation of the name, there are two interpretations.
The first is the etymological explanation by combining the characters.
The three poisons are that which causes affliction;
the mind and spirit are that which is afflicted.
Next, the characters are analyzed individually.
The "afflictions" (kleśa) are that which afflict, and the "objects of affliction" are that which are afflicted;
one should know that this general designation applies to both views (dṛṣṭi) and thought (vitarka).
This is a preliminary classification; below, it will be clarified that within the dull there are those who are sharp.
Just as insects and beasts, so too do ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) give rise to the notion of "self.
Although this "self" is a faculty of sharpness, it belongs to those who are dull-witted;
therefore, it is said that they do not investigate the truth, up to and including their arrogance.
"Crawling" (*ch'üan*) refers to small insects that possess consciousness and are capable of movement.
"Those that raise their stings," etc., refers to the crab family.

The first type has a sting that pervades the entire body;
it is named "Holding a Sword" (Yǒngjiàn) and is also called "Grasping Fire" because its pincers are red.
This is also like the case of the praying mantis blocking the wheel-track and so forth.
"Qí" (鬐) refers to the hair on the neck. The *Shuowen Jiezi* says: [it means the hair on the back of the neck].
The mane and tail are those of a horse.
When wolves and the like become angry, they invariably spread their manes;
it is said that this refers to base creatures such as insects used here as a metaphor for human beings.
If they still harbor such calculations regarding themselves, how much more so regarding others?
As for the phrase "the inferior and base at the bottom," this refers to ordinary persons (pṛthagjana) who possess dull afflictions; yet even among them, there are those with sharp faculties.
Regarding the question "To what extent do the five sharp [faculties] reach? and so forth:
Next, it is explained that within those of sharp faculties there are also those of dull faculties.
For example, various non-Buddhists give rise to anger based on their various views;
this applies to those who have not yet attained meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
Question:
If a follower of the Buddha who practices in successive stages has not yet attained dhyāna,
why is it said that they have abandoned the delusions of view (dṛṣṭi-kleśa) characteristic of a srotāpanna?
Answer:
The present determination of sharp or dull faculties is based on the views that arise in the present moment and the afflictions generated by those views.
This is illustrated by the fact that even if one has not yet attained meditative absorption (dhyāna), all afflictions arising from past habitual tendencies may still manifest.
Furthermore, the arising of the view of self based on the present aggregates still belongs to the dull fetters;
it is that which is abandoned by those in the first fruit and is common to all ordinary worldlings.
Lurking in the depths within the body, it obstructs true outflow-free wisdom (*anāsrava*).
If one perceives the principle of the Truths (*satya*), these afflictions are naturally eliminated;
therefore, this affliction is designated as "view" (*dṛṣṭi*).
Therefore, it is not the same as that which arises after meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
If various non-Buddhists, because they have not yet seen the Truths (*satya*),
attain meditative concentration and thereby sever the dull underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), [the result is still different].
Nevertheless, not even a hair’s breadth of the delusions of view has been severed;
because these delusions of view still manifest,
they differ from those delusions of view that have remained latent or dormant prior to the arising of dhyāna.
Therefore, the eighty-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*) are not taken as the standard for "delusions of view" (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*).
Thus, the meaning of the eighty-eight proclivities is subsumed under the category of the "objects of the aggregates" (*skandha-viṣaya*).
It is only in contrast to and in distinction from those who are sharp or dull [in faculties] that they receive the designation of "view."
Furthermore, this is distinct from the characteristics of the delusions of view that arise after meditative absorption (*dhyāna*).
Here, we are simply distinguishing [this case] from the views that arise subsequent to *dhyāna*;
therefore, it is said: "If one attains *dhyāna* and gives rise to views..."
Even if greed and anger are both included within the category of "gain," it is like the example given below regarding two students:
one who attains [the literal] words is dull-witted, while one who attains the meaning is sharp-witted.
In both cases, they gain mastery over speech and prevail in disputes regarding meaning;
in both cases, they conceive themselves to have attained meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), and their views flourish.
If one were to issue a lower-level distinction to indicate the essential nature of the object (*ālambana-svabhāva*):
Although the eighty-eight afflictions (*anuśaya*) are present within the body,
those that actually arise belong only to the dull afflictions (*mṛdv-anuśaya*) currently active in this sphere.
As for the sharp [afflictions], they are categorized below according to their respective faculties.
First, let us consider their arising.
If there is dullness within the sharp,
then one who has severed the delusions of views is designated as having merely severed the sharp.
This delusion must exist within the dull among the sharp;
for if it were not so, the presence of dullness within the sharp would not be designated as "dull."
Therefore, the next citation from the Abhidharma commentary states:
"Although the sharp exists, the dull belongs to that sharpness;
it arises from the back of the sharp latent tendencies."
Although those of lower capacity give rise to benefit,

Regarding the phrase "if one opens [them]," this next section clarifies the opening and closing [of categories]:
when opened, they become eighty thousand; when closed, they are merely the three poisons.
Since the eighty thousand [afflictions] do not transcend the three poisons,

For this reason, it is necessary to distinguish between their expansion and contraction.
The third section clarifies that the three poisons function as obstacles in different ways.
First, it is explained that all four parts are capable of obstructing meditative concentration (*samādhi*);

That which does not obstruct meditative concentration (samādhi) still belongs to the sphere of the aggregates (skandha).
If it were to obstruct it, the two would belong to different categories.
This refers to whether [the vow] has been generated or not,

The Sūtra, cited below from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, proves that the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) does not constitute an obstruction.
This refers to the distracted mind (*vikṣipta-citta*) entered during the Lion-like Samādhi and others;

Next, according to the perspective of the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*, it is also accepted that all four parts [of the mind] are scattered.
It does not say that all four parts are equally obstructive;
rather, it says that within the state of distraction, there is nothing that does not simultaneously possess associated delusion.
Therefore, it is said that distraction is accompanied by ignorance.
That which can obstruct meditative concentration resides in delusion (*moha*).
If that were so, the opponent’s objection would be established; for in the person who maintains the treatise, all four factors would be equally distracted.
It is associated with both distraction and ignorance;

Delusion necessarily involves hatred and desire.
Since delusion already obstructs concentration,

Yet, it is stated independently that "delusion can obstruct meditative concentration.

The Commentary offers several interpretations:
because their views and afflictions had not yet been eliminated and their great capacity was not yet matured,

Furthermore, the destruction of the afflictions of views employs one unimpeded path and one liberation;

Furthermore, within the two paths, the fetters severed are collectively termed twenty;

Moreover, based on these two types of practitioners, both the views and the afflictions are severed together.

According to the latter interpretation, the twenty are established based on two distinct meanings.
If that is so, the following section clarifies a doubt.
The doubt is as follows:
"If the intention is to discard [the afflictions]..."
If five hundred arhats have indeed abandoned [the outflows],

Although five hundred of them entered the Way through a single gate,
they had not yet distinguished themselves by attaining arhatship; nevertheless,

The pervasive afflictions are like the branches; "branches" refers to the twigs and leaves.

If one were to treat this as "inconceivable," it should be stated that the pervasive afflictions are like flowers and the dharma-nature is like space.
Because of an eye disease, one perceives flowers in empty space.
If one can realize the nature of the disease and know that the flowers are themselves empty, then the emptiness of the flowers and the nature of the disease are identical;
this is the meaning of "perfection" (yuan).
